content.title: About
content.content: Chickpeas are a legume whose seeds are widely used in cuisines around the world. Dried chickpeas with no added fat are fully dehydrated beans ready for further cooking. They have a nutty flavor, firm texture, and a rich nutrient profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chickpeas are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.
Dried chickpeas can be stored for up to a year when kept in proper conditions, retaining their nutritional value.
In India chickpeas are called “chana” and feature in dishes such as chana masala, chaat, and hummus.
Chickpeas are high in protein, making them a popular meat alternative in vegetarian and vegan diets.
There are several varieties – Kabuli, Desi, small, large – each with distinct culinary uses.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas contain about 20 % protein by weight, providing essential amino acids for those who avoid animal products.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs deliver steady energy without causing rapid glucose spikes.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are important for blood formation and preventing anemia, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes dried chickpeas suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chickpeas, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Chickpeas contain phytates that can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting lower their levels.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people; gradual introduction helps the gut adapt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried chickpeas should be soaked in water for at least 8–12 hours, then boiled until tender. They are used in soups, stews, salads, grain bowls, and for making hummus or vegetarian patties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry chickpeas in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold and flavor loss.

content.title: About
content.content: Enfamil NFS is an infant formula for newborns and babies up to 6 months, formulated according to WHO recommendations. It provides an optimal balance of proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals needed for growth and development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The formula is enriched with DHA and ARA – fatty acids important for brain and eye development.
It contains prebiotics to support a healthy gut microbiome.
Enfamil NFS is manufactured in the USA under strict quality and safety standards.
The composition meets the required levels of iron, zinc, and vitamin D for infants.

items.title: Supports growth
items.content: Balanced protein and energy content promotes normal weight gain and linear growth.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA aid the development of the central nervous system and visual function.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Vitamin D and calcium help build strong bone tissue.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C and zinc strengthen the infant’s immune system.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Prebiotics foster beneficial gut bacteria, improving digestion.

items.title: Cow‑milk protein allergy
items.content: Some infants may develop an allergy to cow’s milk protein; discontinue use if symptoms appear.

items.title: Improper mixing
items.content: Over‑concentrated or overly diluted formula can lead to dehydration or over‑feeding.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, the formula should be used within 48 hours to maintain quality.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Mix the specified amount of powder with clean, boiled water, cool to room temperature, and feed the baby immediately. Do not heat the prepared bottle in a microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry formula in a cool, dry place away from direct light. Keep the container tightly sealed after opening and use within 48 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Breaded meatballs are small balls made from ground meat (commonly beef, pork, or a blend) that are coated in a crispy breadcrumb crust and served with a savory gravy. They are quick to prepare and work well as a main dish or a convenient snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meatballs originated in medieval Europe as a way to use leftover meat.
The breadcrumb coating helps retain moisture, keeping the interior juicy.
Traditional gravy is made from stock, cream, and spices, giving a rich flavor.
In Russia, meatballs are often paired with mashed potatoes or pasta.
Variations include chicken, turkey, veal, or even vegetarian versions made from legumes.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B12 and B6 support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Zinc present in meat helps maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein and fat makes the dish a good source of sustained energy.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Using fatty ground meat and a thick breadcrumb coating can increase calorie count.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Breadcrumbs contain wheat, which is important for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Meat must be cooked thoroughly to avoid salmonella and other pathogens.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared gravies often contain salt; those monitoring blood pressure should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hot meatballs drenched in gravy. They pair well with mashed potatoes, rice, pasta, or fresh vegetables. For a lighter option, bake them in the oven instead of frying.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked meatballs in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Pepperoni is a spicy cured sausage made from pork and beef, seasoned with paprika, garlic, pepper and other spices. It is commonly used on pizza, sandwiches and as a snack. Pepperoni has a bright red color and a distinctive smoky, aromatic flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pepperoni originated in the United States as an adaptation of Italian salami, but with a brighter flavor and color.
Traditionally pepperoni is smoked, giving it its characteristic aroma.
In the U.S. more than 3 million tons of pepperoni are consumed each year, mostly on pizza.
Capsaicin content makes pepperoni one of the spiciest popular sausages.
Vegetarian pepperoni versions exist, made from soy protein and flavorings.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pepperoni provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: The red meat in pepperoni supplies a notable amount of heme iron, essential for oxygen transport.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pepperoni contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc from pepperoni supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Moderate amount of fats
items.content: Most fats in pepperoni are monounsaturated and polyunsaturated, which can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pepperoni is often salty; excess sodium can raise blood pressure and strain the kidneys.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: The product contains saturated fats, which should be limited in cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to pork or beef proteins.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Nitrites are commonly used to preserve color and shelf life; high intake is considered potentially harmful.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pepperoni is usually sliced thin and used as a pizza topping, added to pasta, salads, sandwiches, or fried as a snack. It can also be baked until crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pepperoni in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 weeks. For longer storage freeze it in a bag at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for up to 3 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or color change.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato fries are strips of batata (Ipomoea batatas) that are deep‑fried or baked until crisp. The tuber, native to Central and South America, has a naturally sweet flavor and bright orange flesh rich in beta‑carotene.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes contain two to three times more beta‑carotene than regular potatoes.
Sweet potato fries are often offered in fast‑food chains as a more nutritious alternative to classic fries.
Batata comes in several colors: orange, purple, yellow and white.
Unlike regular potatoes, sweet potatoes have a lower glycemic index, especially when baked.
The word “fries” comes from the French “frites,” meaning fried.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium maintains electrolyte balance, normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Sweet potatoes provide anthocyanins and vitamin C, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in fat when baked
items.content: Baked sweet potato fries contain less saturated fat than traditional deep‑fried versions.

items.title: High carbohydrate content
items.content: Sweet potatoes are carbohydrate‑dense, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Allergy to sweet potato
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to sweet potato.

items.title: Acrylamide formation during frying
items.content: Prolonged high‑temperature frying can produce acrylamides, compounds of potential concern.

items.title: Foodborne risk if stored improperly
items.content: Cut strips oxidize quickly and can harbor bacteria if left at room temperature for too long.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweet potato fries are served hot as a side, snack, or accompaniment to main dishes. Sprinkle with salt, paprika, garlic powder or herbs. For a healthier option, bake the strips at 200 °C for 20‑25 minutes, turning halfway through.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked fries in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Raw sweet potatoes keep best in a cool, dry place; sliced strips can be kept in water in the fridge, changing the water every 12 hours to prevent discoloration.
